answers.text: Three lines for the driver's message every time, same order — drop-off time, pallet count, damage noted. 24-hour time, pallet count as a number, 'none noted' if nothing's said. If any of the three is missing, write 'not stated' rather than skip it.

Same four columns every time — time, customer, topic, outcome — plus the follow-up count at the top, counting only 'call back' or 'no answer'. If the same customer shows up twice for the same topic, I'd list it once and note it happened twice, not count it twice.

Doesn't add up — it's not the crew or the six hours, it's the finishing day. Access from 8am on the 22nd plus six hours finishes early afternoon the 22nd itself, not the 23rd as the note claims — a full day off.
9 out of 118 late works out to about 92%, that part's right. But 96 to 118 is nearer 23%, not the 20% given, so that figure's wrong.

I'd sign off Output 2, the one with 940 and 827 shown, not just 88%. Output 1 gives only the percentage, nothing behind it to check. The 88% might well be right, but there's no way to know without running the count myself.

I'd send Email 2 as is — the volume figures, 1,200 up to 1,650, are right there to check. Email 1 just says 'we'd expect a better rate' with no number behind it, so there's nothing to check that claim against. That doesn't make Email 1 wrong, the ask could still be fair, it's just not shown. Before sending Email 1, I'd pull the real order volume from the PO log and put actual numbers in, rather than send it on tone alone.

1. Vendor pricing — no, that's the vendor's own confidential detail, not for an unvetted tool. 2. Procurement spend, aggregate — yes, no vendor names in it. 3. Unsigned budget draft — no, that's internal and not released yet. 4. Vendor datasheet — yes, already public on their site, so no reason to hold it back. 5. Employee's home address — no, that's personal information.

Hourly rates and retainer cap I'd hold back, that's commercial detail for a tool we haven't checked. The NDA clause needs the same caution, it names the client directly. The service scope by itself is fine to paste though, it's just describing the work.
I'd have the monthly totals cross-checked against the warehouse system directly before the summary reaches finance at month-end. That would catch a wrong total or a made-up line, not just a typo.

Step 1 is the one that worries me, since a misread invoice carries the wrong numbers through everything downstream. But the real gate needs to sit at step 4, the automatic submission, because that's the point where nothing can be undone. The gate should flag anything where the PO match sits close to the tolerance limit, or the total looks unusually high, not just a general review. If it gets flagged, it should go to whoever handles that supplier for a manual look, not sit there unsubmitted with no one told.
